subject: english-literature
topicDisplay: Paper 1 Love Through The Ages Drama Prose Poetry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The Renaissance 'cruel mistress' figure in love poetry functions to:
options: Replace the speaker as the poem's voice
Reward the lover's devotion at once
Withhold favour, prompting the lover's complaint and intensified longing
Narrate a battle scene
questions.explain: The cruel, withholding mistress generates the poetry of frustrated desire and complaint.

questions.q: The phrase 'love through the ages' invites study of how:
options: Only one definitive view of love exists for all time
Context is irrelevant to love texts
Conventions and representations of love evolve with shifting social and historical values
Love poetry stopped being written after the Romantics
questions.explain: The topic examines change and continuity in how love is represented across different periods.

questions.q: In scansion, a foot of two consecutive stressed syllables is called a:
options: Pyrrhic
Anapaest
Spondee
Trochee
questions.explain: A spondee consists of two stressed syllables, often used to slow or weight a line.

questions.q: Across periods, the relationship between love and 'mutability' (change/transience) is a key concern because poets repeatedly confront:
options: The threat that time, ageing and death pose to love, prompting carpe diem or claims of poetic immortality
The impossibility of writing about love
The irrelevance of time to love
The permanence of all human feeling
questions.explain: Mutability drives both carpe diem urgency and the rival boast that verse can immortalise love beyond time.

questions.q: The distinction between the 'poetic voice' (or speaker) and the poet matters because:
options: Only sonnets have a speaker
The poet and speaker are by definition the same person
Poems never have a speaker
The speaker is always a fictional construct who can differ from the poet
questions.explain: A-level analysis treats the speaker as a constructed voice, which may be ironic, dramatic or distinct from the author.

questions.q: A trochee is a metrical foot consisting of:
options: An unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable
Three syllables stressed on the first
Two unstressed syllables
A stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable
questions.explain: A trochee reverses the iamb: a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one.

questions.q: When comparing two poems' methods and ideas, the most analytically rewarding approach is to:
options: Decide which poet was more famous
Describe one poem fully, then the other, with no link
Compare how each poet uses form and language to treat a shared concern, weighing similarity and difference
List the rhyme schemes only
questions.explain: Effective comparison is integrated, examining how each text's methods shape its treatment of a common theme.

questions.q: A feminist re-reading of a Renaissance love sonnet would most likely emphasise:
options: The number of lines in the poem
How the woman is silenced or objectified, and whose voice and power the poem privileges
The poet's choice of rhyme scheme alone
The poet's exact birthplace
questions.explain: Feminist criticism foregrounds gendered power, voice and objectification within the text.

questions.q: In love poetry, the 'complaint' or 'lament' tradition gives voice to:
options: A speaker grieving over rejection, absence or the cruelty of the beloved
A satirist mocking metre
A triumphant lover celebrating success
A neutral observer cataloguing weather
questions.explain: The amatory complaint expresses the suffering of the rejected, neglected or longing lover.

questions.q: Across the 'love through the ages' span, representations of marriage shift partly because:
options: Poets stopped writing about marriage entirely after 1600
All periods treated marriage identically
Marriage was never a literary subject
Marriage law and women's social/economic status changed over the centuries
questions.explain: Changing legal, economic and social conditions for women reshape how marriage is represented across periods.

questions.q: When a sentence runs on past the end of a line of verse without punctuation or pause, the technique is:
options: End-stopping
Caesura
Enjambment
Anaphora
questions.explain: Enjambment carries the sense over the line break, while end-stopping closes a line with a pause.

questions.q: A defining preoccupation of Romantic poetry (Wordsworth, Coleridge, Keats) is:
options: The imagination, nature and intense subjective feeling
Neoclassical decorum and satire
Industrial reportage in plain prose
Strict adherence to the three dramatic unities
questions.explain: Romanticism foregrounds imagination, nature, emotion and the individual sensibility against Enlightenment rationalism.

questions.q: Much contemporary (post-2000) poetry tends to favour:
options: Latin epic conventions
Flexible free verse, colloquial registers and diverse, often personal or political voices
Strict adherence to fixed classical forms only
Exclusively the heroic couplet
questions.explain: Contemporary poetry commonly draws on free verse, everyday speech and a plurality of voices and concerns.

questions.q: Donne's 'The Sun Rising' treats love through which characteristic Metaphysical move?
options: A bold conceit in which the lovers' bedroom becomes the centre of the whole universe
A renunciation of physical desire
A simple pastoral celebration of shepherds
A modest, plain-spoken understatement
questions.explain: Donne hyperbolically argues the lovers contain everything, making their room the world's centre, a typical conceit.

questions.q: Reading love poetry across the ages, a 'feminist' approach differs from a 'traditional' one chiefly by:
options: Caring only about rhyme schemes
Questioning the gendered power, voice and objectification the conventions encode
Refusing to read pre-1900 texts
Treating all love poems as identical
questions.explain: Feminist reading interrogates how love conventions encode and naturalise gendered power and the objectification of women.

questions.q: A line of iambic pentameter contains how many metrical feet, and of what basic pattern?
options: Five feet, each an unstressed-then-stressed iamb
Six feet, each a stressed-then-unstressed trochee
Five feet, each a dactyl
Four feet, each a spondee
questions.explain: Iambic pentameter is five iambs per line, each iamb being an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one.

questions.q: A poem's 'form' and its 'structure' are distinguished in that form refers to the fixed type or shape, while structure refers to:
options: The poet's date of birth
The internal organisation and development of ideas across the poem
The number of letters in the title
The colour of imagery only
questions.explain: Form is the recognisable type (sonnet, ode), whereas structure concerns how the argument or feeling unfolds and is ordered.

questions.q: In Andrew Marvell's 'To His Coy Mistress', the argument's logical structure ('Had we but world enough... But... Now therefore') resembles:
options: A villanelle's refrain pattern
A three-stage syllogistic seduction: if we had time, but we don't, therefore act now
An elegy in four parts
A pastoral lullaby
questions.explain: The poem proceeds like a syllogism, moving from hypothetical leisure to the pressure of time to a 'therefore' urging action.

questions.q: An ode is traditionally a poem that is:
options: A 14-line love poem with a couplet
A serious, elevated lyric addressed to a person, thing or abstraction
A brief, witty epigram of two lines
A narrative folk song with a refrain
questions.explain: The ode is a dignified, often celebratory lyric of address, as in Keats's odes to a nightingale or a Grecian urn.

questions.q: The repetition of consonant sounds, especially at the ends or middles of words, as in 'pitter-patter', is:
options: Assonance
Sibilance
Cacophony
Consonance
questions.explain: Consonance is the repetition of consonant sounds; assonance, by contrast, repeats vowel sounds.

questions.q: A villanelle is a fixed form notable for which feature?
options: An unrhymed line of five iambic feet
Fourteen lines split into octave and sestet
A single eight-line stanza with a couplet turn
Two refrains repeated across nineteen lines in five tercets and a quatrain
questions.explain: The villanelle has nineteen lines, five tercets and a closing quatrain, woven around two recurring refrains.

questions.q: 'Courtly love', a medieval convention shaping later love poetry, characteristically presents the lover as:
options: A humble servant devoted to an idealised, often unattainable lady
A wealthy suitor negotiating a dowry
A rival seeking to humiliate the beloved
An indifferent master commanding his lady
questions.explain: Courtly love casts the male lover as a worshipful servant to a distant, idealised lady, often a married noblewoman.

questions.q: The concept of the 'male gaze', often applied in feminist re-readings of love poetry, draws attention to how:
options: Women poets dominated the love tradition
Love poetry avoids describing women
Men were excluded from writing love poetry
The female beloved is frequently positioned as a passive object of male desire and viewing
questions.explain: The male gaze frames the woman as the object to be looked at and desired, a perspective feminist critics interrogate.

questions.q: 'Unrequited love' as a convention denotes a love that is:
options: Felt by one party but not returned by the other
Returned and fulfilled in marriage
Forbidden by law
Purely spiritual and divine
questions.explain: Unrequited love is love that is not reciprocated, a long-standing source of lyric longing.

questions.q: Rhyme that occurs within a single line rather than at line-endings is called:
options: Internal rhyme
End rhyme
Eye rhyme
Masculine rhyme
questions.explain: Internal rhyme places rhyming words within the same line, adding density and momentum.

questions.q: Blank verse is best defined as:
options: Verse with no fixed metre or line length
Rhyming couplets in iambic pentameter
Unrhymed iambic pentameter
Verse arranged in three-line stanzas
questions.explain: Blank verse is unrhymed iambic pentameter, the staple metre of much English dramatic and narrative poetry.

questions.q: A ballad is a verse form most characteristically defined by:
options: Free verse with no stanza divisions
A single unbroken stanza of fourteen lines
A narrative told in quatrains, often with refrain and a song-like rhythm
Strict iambic pentameter throughout with no rhyme
questions.explain: The ballad narrates a story in quatrains, traditionally with a strong, song-like beat and frequent refrain.

questions.q: In approaching an unseen poem, the soundest opening method is to:
options: Assume the speaker is identical to the poet
Decide the poet's biography before reading
Read closely for how form, language and structure shape meaning, not just paraphrase the content
Count only the syllables and stop there
questions.explain: Strong unseen analysis links technique (form, language, structure, sound) to meaning rather than merely summarising.

questions.q: A poem spoken throughout by a single character who is not the poet, addressing a silent listener, is a:
options: Villanelle
Petrarchan sonnet
Pastoral elegy
Dramatic monologue
questions.explain: The dramatic monologue, perfected by Browning, has one speaker distinct from the poet revealing themselves to a silent auditor.

questions.q: The carpe diem tradition in love poetry, exemplified by Marvell's 'To His Coy Mistress', urges the beloved to:
options: Renounce earthly desire for spiritual love
Wait patiently for marriage
Mourn a love already lost
Seize the day and yield to love before time and death intervene
questions.explain: Carpe diem means 'seize the day', pressing the beloved to act on desire because time is short.
